title: Cost and Price Videos
article_body:
The Cost and Price Video is the first of The Selling 7, and it belongs first because pricing is almost always the first real question a prospect has. You may have already addressed cost in written content — a blog post, a pricing page, or an FAQ. The Cost and Price Video takes that same transparency and brings it to life on camera, where tone, explanation, and personality can do things a written page cannot.

The strategic value of this video is simple: a salesperson can share it with a prospect before a discovery call. Instead of walking into that call cold — with pricing uncertainty already creating friction — the prospect arrives having watched your rep or a company leader explain cost honestly, in their own words, to every decision-maker involved in the purchase. No secondhand summaries. No misquoted numbers. Just a clear, direct explanation they can pause, rewatch, and share internally.

## What Belongs in the Video

A well-made Cost and Price Video covers three things. First, it addresses the factors that influence what your product or service costs — materials, labor, scope, customization, geography, or whatever actually drives the number in your business. Second, it puts your pricing in market context, explaining why similar products or services can vary widely in price and what separates a cheaper option from a more expensive one. Third, it makes the case for your own pricing — not defensively, but clearly, explaining what buyers get for what they pay.

The goal is not to close the sale in the video. The goal is to eliminate the anxious, half-formed question about cost that sits in every prospect's mind and replace it with a clear, honest answer. Buyers who feel they understand your pricing before a call are buyers who arrive with their guard down. They're ready to talk about fit rather than fencing over numbers.

## One Video Per Product or Service

If your company offers multiple main products or services, create a separate Cost and Price Video for each one. A single video that tries to cover everything becomes too vague to be useful. A prospect evaluating your enterprise software package and a prospect evaluating your entry-level plan have different questions, and each deserves a direct answer. Specificity is what makes these videos effective in an actual sales conversation.

## How Long Should It Be?

Most Cost and Price Videos run five to eight minutes. That is long enough to be genuinely thorough and short enough to hold the attention of a motivated buyer who actually wants to understand what they're about to spend. Do not pad the video to hit a target length, and do not cut it short to seem concise. Follow the content. If your offering is straightforward, five minutes may be plenty. If it involves significant complexity, customization, or comparison with competitors, take the time the topic requires.

## Production and Delivery

These videos do not need to be over-produced. A clear image, good audio, and a genuine on-camera presence from someone the prospect will actually meet are more valuable than high-end graphics. What prospects want is to feel like they're getting a real conversation with someone honest, not a polished pitch from a company trying to hide something.

Once created, these videos are deployed through Assignment Selling — shared by a salesperson in a one-to-one video message or email before a scheduled call. They also belong on relevant product and service pages on your website, where prospects doing their own research can find them. The same transparency that builds trust in a sales conversation builds trust in organic search.

The Cost and Price Video is one of the highest-leverage investments a company can make in its video strategy. It directly addresses the single most common reason a sales conversation breaks down before it begins. Make it honest. Make it specific. And put it to work.

key_questions.question: Why make a video about cost when I already have a pricing page?
key_questions.answer: A written pricing page and a cost video serve different jobs. The pricing page is found through search. The video is shared by your salesperson directly with a specific prospect before a call. It allows your rep to explain nuance, context, and value in a way that a static page cannot, and it ensures every decision-maker hears the same message in your own words.

key_questions.question: What should a Cost and Price Video actually cover?
key_questions.answer: Three things: the factors that influence the cost of your product or service, how prices vary in your market and why, and why your product costs what it does — your value proposition explained plainly. Avoid vagueness. The goal is to leave no honest question unanswered.

key_questions.question: How long should a Cost and Price Video be?
key_questions.answer: Long enough to be thorough, short enough to stay focused. Most run five to eight minutes. If you have a simple product, it might be shorter. A highly complex offering might need more time. Follow the content, not a target runtime.

key_questions.question: Do I need separate videos for each product or service?
key_questions.answer: Yes. Each major product or service deserves its own video. A single video trying to cover all your offerings becomes too general to help anyone. Specificity is what makes these videos useful in a real sales conversation.

key_questions.question: Who should appear in a Cost and Price Video?
key_questions.answer: Ideally someone the prospect will also speak with — a salesperson, a company leader, or a subject matter expert. The goal is to make the video feel like a direct conversation rather than a corporate production. Authenticity matters more than production polish.
